newsitem.title: DUBAI: UK nurses appear in first Saudi murder hearing.
newsitem.headline: UK nurses appear in first Saudi murder hearing.

text.p: The attorney representing the family of an Australian nurse murdered in Saudi Arabia on Monday demanded the death penalty for two British colleagues charged with killing her, the two women's lawyer said.

The law firm of Salah al-Hejailan said in a statement its clients, Deborah Parry, 41, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, appeared before a panel of three judges at the first hearing into the case at an Islamic sharia court.
"The nurses appeared nervous but controlled," it said.

Both nurses have been charged with the murder of Yvonne Gilford, 55, in her dormitory room at the King Fahd medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dhahran on December 11. She had been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.

The women have been imprisoned in the nearby city of Dammam since December. If convicted of murder, they could face public beheading by the sword, the first time Western women would have been executed in the conservative Islamic kingdom.

"The lawyer representing the Australian family demanded the death penalty for the two nurses. When asked by the judges on what this demand was based the lawyer stated only that he relied on the written statements made by the nurses," said Hejailan's statement, faxed to Reuters.
Saudi police said the nurses confessed to the murder and the confessions had been filed with Saudi judges.
Lawyers representing the victim's family were not available for comment.
"The court commenced an investigation into the evidence after both nurses denied having been involved in any way in the tragic death of the Australian nurse," said Hejailan's three-page statement.
"The court began to hear evidence as to the circumstances in which the two British nurses made written statements while in police custody and which they have subsequently withdrawn".
Hejailan's firm said the women had withdrawn confessions, and one of them retracted a statement that she had a lesbian relationship with the victim.

"Our clients have withdrawn the written statements given in the days following their arrests without the benefit of counsel and without access to British diplomatic staff," said the statement. "In essence, our clients maintain that they did not kill Ms. Gilford and know nothing about events surrounding" it.
The public prosecutor did not attend Monday's preliminary hearing session and the case was adjourned until Tuesday, Hejailan's statement said.
Gilford's family in Australia have ruled out clemency, saying the two should face the maximum punishment.
Legal experts said if they were found guilty of manslaughter rather than murder the nurses would not be condemned to death.
